skill.name: provider-management
skill.description: Manage AI provider authentication, priorities, usage limits, and fallback routing across major model providers.
skill.summary: Configure provider credentials, priorities, limits, and fallback behavior for multi-model AI workflows.
skill.author: AttendantLion8

security_audit.summary: Most static external-command findings are false positives caused by Markdown inline code and fenced slash-command examples. The security-relevant issues are the documented hidden home-directory credential store and the skill flow that asks users to provide API keys, session tokens, and OAuth secrets.

remediation.issue: Credential storage in a hidden home directory
remediation.suggestion: Document exact file permissions, encrypt tokens at rest when possible, and restrict reads and writes to ~/.opencode/provider-fallback/ only.

remediation.issue: API keys and subscription tokens are entered through commands
remediation.suggestion: Require explicit user confirmation before storing secrets, and redact keys, client secrets, and session tokens from logs and transcripts.

remediation.issue: Slash-command examples are formatted as bash blocks
remediation.suggestion: Mark slash command blocks as examples or plain text when they are not shell commands, so scanners and users do not mistake them for executable shell code.

SKILL.md directs configuration under ~/.opencode/provider-fallback/ and lists auth.json and tokens.json for credentials. A community skill that stores secrets in a hidden home directory is a real sensitive filesystem risk even when documented.

The documented hidden directory is intended for persistent provider configuration and credential storage. Hidden file access is legitimate for app config, but security relevant because it includes auth and OAuth token files.
The line is troubleshooting text about token expiry, not host or system reconnaissance. It does not instruct collecting OS, network, hardware, or account inventory details.

content.value_statement: Teams often juggle subscriptions, OAuth accounts, and API keys across model providers. This skill organizes priorities, limits, and fallback choices in one workflow.
actual_capabilities: Documents provider priority across subscription, OAuth, and API authentication methods.
Lists supported Claude, GPT, Gemini, Grok, Llama, DeepSeek, Mistral, Cohere, and Qwen model families.
Shows slash commands for provider authentication, model lookup, priority ordering, limits, status, and switching.
Explains local configuration files for priorities, usage tracking, credentials, and OAuth tokens.
Describes fallback selection based on auth priority, usage capacity, and provider-specific model IDs.
limitations: The skill file is documentation only; it does not include executable command implementations.
It requires users to manage sensitive provider credentials and tokens.
Provider model names and availability can change outside the skill.
It does not prove encryption or key-management behavior for stored credentials.

use_cases.description: Define priority order and fallback behavior for teams that use multiple AI providers.

use_cases.title: Map Model Names
use_cases.description: Find canonical model names and provider-specific IDs before changing application settings.

use_cases.title: Control Usage Limits
use_cases.description: Set daily and monthly limits to reduce surprise spending across shared provider accounts.

prompt_templates.title: Plan Authentication Setup
prompt_templates.prompt: Use provider-management to design a setup for Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google with subscription first, OAuth second, and API keys last.

prompt_templates.title: Tune Fallback Priorities
prompt_templates.prompt: Use provider-management to propose provider-priority and provider-limits settings for a high-reliability coding workflow with monthly budget limits.

prompt_templates.title: Audit Provider Configuration
prompt_templates.prompt: Use provider-management to review my provider order, usage limits, and credential storage plan for security and cost risks.

output_examples.input: Show provider status for a multi-vendor setup.
output_examples.output: A concise status summary grouped by provider, authentication method, priority, and remaining usage capacity.

output_examples.input: Choose a fallback order for Claude workloads.
output_examples.output: Recommended order: subscription first, OAuth second, API key fallback, then Bedrock or Vertex when local limits are near capacity.
A checklist covering token expiry, refresh behavior, storage location, and actions needed before reconnecting providers.

best_practices: Configure subscription access first, then OAuth, then API keys as fallback.
Set limits below real quotas to leave room for manual recovery.
Keep provider credentials in restricted files and rotate tokens on a schedule.
anti_patterns: Do not paste raw keys into shared chats, logs, or issue trackers.
Do not rely on one provider when uptime matters.
Do not enable automatic switching without clear spending limits.

faq.question: Does it run provider commands by itself?
faq.answer: No. The reviewed skill file documents commands and workflows. It does not include executable implementation files.

faq.question: Which tools support it?
faq.answer: The report lists Claude, Codex, and Claude Code as supported tools.

faq.question: Does it store credentials?
faq.answer: The skill describes auth.json and tokens.json under ~/.opencode/provider-fallback/. Treat those files as sensitive.

faq.question: Can it choose the best provider automatically?
faq.answer: It describes a flow that sorts providers by auth priority, usage capacity, and model ID mapping.

faq.question: What should I configure first?
faq.answer: Start with subscription access, add OAuth, then add API keys as fallback.

faq.question: Are provider lists guaranteed current?
faq.answer: No. Check provider documentation because model IDs and availability change over time.
